content.diagnostic_criteria: A. ≥5 symptoms during the same 2-week period, representing a change from previous functioning, with at least one being depressed mood or markedly diminished interest/pleasure: (1) depressed mood; (2) markedly diminished interest/pleasure; (3) significant weight/appetite change; (4) insomnia/hypersomnia; (5) psychomotor agitation/retardation; (6) fatigue/loss of energy; (7) feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; (8) diminished ability to think/concentrate or indecisiveness; (9) recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, plan, or attempt. B. Symptoms cause distress/impairment. C. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. D. Not better explained by schizoaffective/schizophrenia spectrum disorders. E. No history of manic or hypomanic episode.
content.prevalence: 12-month prevalence ~7% adults; higher in females. Substantial global burden with high recurrence and disability.
content.age_of_onset: Peak onset late adolescence to mid-20s; can occur across the lifespan.
content.prognosis: Course ranges from single episode to recurrent/chronic. Early treatment, full remission, and maintenance reduce relapse/recurrence and suicide risk. Comorbidity (anxiety, substance use, medical illness) and psychosocial stress worsen outcomes.

circuitry: Dysfunction in fronto-limbic networks (prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, amygdala, hippocampus) affecting emotion regulation and cognitive control.
Default mode network hyperconnectivity with reduced task-positive network engagement; altered reward circuitry in ventral striatum.
neurochemistry: Glutamate/GABA imbalance; neurotrophic factors (e.g., BDNF) reduced during episodes; HPA-axis dysregulation and inflammatory cytokine elevations.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Polygenic vulnerability interacting with adverse life events, chronic stress, sleep disruption, and medical comorbidity.

history_psychosocial: Episode timeline, triggers, prior episodes/treatments, suicidality/self-harm, psychosis, catatonia, peripartum or seasonal pattern.
Function across school/work/home; substance use; trauma history; sleep, pain, and medical comorbidities.
medical_assessment: Screen labs when indicated: CBC (anemia), CMP, TSH/free T4; B12/folate, HbA1c, lipids; pregnancy test if applicable.
Consider sleep apnea screening, ECG if cardiac risk/antipsychotic or TCA use.
standardized_measures: PHQ-9 or HAM-D for severity/monitoring; GAD-7 for anxiety.
C-SSRS for suicide risk; MoCA if cognitive complaints prominent.
risk_stratification: Urgent evaluation/higher level of care for active suicidal intent/plan, psychosis, catatonia, severe dehydration/weight loss, or inability to care for self.
differential_diagnosis: Bipolar depression (screen for past hypomania/mania), persistent depressive disorder, adjustment disorder, grief, substance/medication-induced depression, neurocognitive disorder, hypothyroidism and other medical causes.
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaborative care among primary care, psychiatry, psychotherapy, and when needed sleep/pain specialists; include family/supports (with consent) for safety and adherence.

psychotic_possible: Mood-congruent or incongruent delusions/hallucinations in severe cases

severity_levels.mild: Few symptoms beyond diagnostic threshold, minor impairment.
severity_levels.moderate: Symptoms and impairment between mild and severe.
severity_levels.severe: Many symptoms, marked impairment; psychotic features or high suicide risk may be present.

biological: Chronic medical illness, pain, sleep disorders
psychological: High neuroticism, perfectionism, negative attributional style
environmental: Substance use, shift work, circadian disruption

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism, presenteeism, reduced productivity and errors.
impact_on_life.medical: Poor adherence to treatments, worsened outcomes, increased healthcare utilization.

comorbidities: Anxiety disorders (GAD, panic, social anxiety, PTSD)

psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention.
Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) — role disputes/transitions, grief, social support.
Behavioral Activation (BA) — structured activity scheduling and reward re-engagement.
Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (ACT) or Mindfulness-Based CBT as adjuncts.
Family/couples therapy when relational stressors contribute.
medications: First-line antidepressants: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram).
SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, levomilnacipran) — consider if pain/fatigue prominent; monitor blood pressure.
Bupropion — energizing, fewer sexual side effects; avoid in seizure/eating disorders.
Mirtazapine — helpful for insomnia, low appetite/weight loss.
Tricyclics (e.g., nortriptyline) and MAOIs — effective but second/third-line due to side-effect and interaction profiles.

Augmentation for partial response: aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, quetiapine XR; lithium (suicide risk reduction); liothyronine (T3) in selected cases; buspirone or bupropion combo; psychostimulants/modafinil for residual fatigue (specialist-guided).
Peripartum: weigh maternal-fetal risks/benefits; sertraline often favored; coordinate with obstetrics.
Geriatrics: start low/go slow; monitor hyponatremia; consider QTc with citalopram; watch drug interactions.
neuromodulation: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or treatment-resistant depression, or urgent suicidality.
Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) for treatment-resistant cases.
Ketamine/esketamine (under REMS/clinic protocols) for treatment-resistant depression or acute suicidal ideation.
Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) in highly refractory chronic depression (specialist-guided).
lifestyle_interventions: Sleep hygiene and circadian regularity; CBT-I when indicated.
Regular aerobic activity and structured daily routines.
Nutrition supporting metabolic health; limit alcohol/cannabis.
Social rhythm stabilization; problem-solving for stressors; digital mood tracking.
care_coordination: Collaborative care linking primary care and behavioral health.
Safety planning for suicidality; means restriction counseling.
Monitor side effects and labs (e.g., metabolic panels for SGAs, lithium levels/renal/thyroid when used).

treatment_goals: Achieve full symptom remission and functional recovery.
Prevent relapse/recurrence with continuation and maintenance strategies.
Reduce suicide risk and address comorbidities.
Improve quality of life, sleep, and role functioning.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Presenting chiefly with somatic complaints (pain, fatigue, GI) in primary care.
Assuming symptoms are normal grief, burnout, or personality without assessing criteria and impairment.
Unrecognized bipolar spectrum — inadequate screening for past hypomania leading to antidepressant monotherapy risks.
overdiagnosis_factors: Transient stress reactions or adjustment disorder labeled as MDD without full criteria/duration.
Bereavement or cultural/religious mourning incorrectly pathologized.
Cognitive effects of medications/medical illness mistaken for depression without mood/anhedonia.
warning_signs: Escalating suicidal ideation, planning, or rehearsal.
New psychotic features, catatonia, or failure to maintain nutrition/hydration.
self_help_strategies: Daily routine with scheduled pleasant activities and gradual activation.
Sleep regularity; limit long naps; consistent wake time.
Peer support, problem-solving steps for stressors, and values-aligned goals.
Use reminders/pill organizers; attend follow-ups and share safety plan with supports.

adolescence: Irritable mood more prominent; school decline and social withdrawal; coordinate school supports and family engagement.
adulthood: Work impairment, parenting stress; integrate workplace accommodations and couples/family interventions when relevant.
older_adults: More somatic/cognitive symptoms; higher medical comorbidity; favor SSRIs with safer profiles; monitor hyponatremia and falls.
peripartum: Onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum; screen for safety, bonding difficulties; coordinate obstetrics/pediatrics.

real_life_examples.person: A high-performing 34-year-old accountant who prided herself on reliability began arriving late to work, missing deadlines she would never have overlooked before. She stopped answering friends' calls and spent evenings staring at the TV without watching. Her partner noticed she was picking at meals and staying awake until 3 a.m. scrolling her phone. After weeks of this, she told her supervisor she couldn't focus on the simplest spreadsheets anymore. Her team began covering for her errors, and she received her first written warning. She withdrew further, convinced she was incompetent and a burden, and stopped opening her work laptop altogether.

A 16-year-old who loved basketball suddenly quit the team mid-season without explanation. His parents assumed it was typical teen moodiness until his grades dropped from A's to D's within a month. He stopped joking with his younger siblings and snapped at his mom over small things like dinner questions. His sleep flipped: he'd lie awake until dawn, then sleep through alarms. When his dad asked what was wrong, he said, 'Nothing matters. Leave me alone.' He stopped showering regularly, wore the same hoodie daily, and his friends eventually stopped texting. His parents found searches for 'ways to disappear' on his laptop.

A 52-year-old librarian known for her warmth and book recommendations started calling in sick two or three days a week. Colleagues noticed she looked exhausted and had stopped bringing her usual homemade lunches. She began making careless cataloging mistakes and seemed irritated by patron questions she used to enjoy. At home, she stopped gardening, let dishes pile up, and told her husband everything felt pointless. She gained weight from eating cereal for every meal and sleeping 12 hours a night but still feeling drained. Eventually, she stopped going to work entirely, telling HR she'd resign because she was 'useless.'

A 29-year-old software engineer who was once the life of team happy hours stopped attending altogether. He started missing stand-ups and replying to Slack messages hours late with one-word answers. His manager noticed his code commits dropped off, and when asked, he said he couldn't think clearly anymore. He stopped seeing his girlfriend, canceled their vacation, and spent weekends lying in bed scrolling but not reading. He lost 15 pounds because eating felt like a chore. His roommate heard him pacing the apartment at night. One day he didn't show up to an important demo, and HR called for a welfare check.

A 68-year-old retired teacher who had been active in her church choir and book club began complaining of constant back pain and headaches. She saw her doctor repeatedly but tests showed nothing. She stopped attending Sunday services and book club meetings, saying she was too tired. Her daughter noticed the refrigerator was nearly empty and her mother was losing weight. She seemed confused sometimes, repeating questions and forgetting conversations. She told her daughter, 'I'm just old and useless now,' and spent most days in her recliner. Her daughter assumed it was normal aging until her mother stopped answering the phone for days.

content.when_to_seek_help: Immediate help for suicidal thoughts/intent, psychosis, catatonia, or inability to care for self. Prompt evaluation for persistent low mood/anhedonia ≥2 weeks with impairment, especially if recurrent or with medical comorbidity.

positive_factors: Early, adequate dose/duration of treatment and adherence
Strong social support and engagement in psychotherapy
challenging_factors: Comorbid anxiety/substance use, chronic medical illness, or personality pathology
Treatment resistance, residual symptoms, or rapid relapse after remission
Ongoing psychosocial adversity or unstable housing/employment

aeo.what_is: A condition causing persistent low mood and loss of interest that significantly disrupts daily life and functioning.

content.temporal_criteria: Symptoms must persist most of the day, nearly every day for at least two weeks and represent a clear change from previous functioning. Episodes can be single or recurrent, and without treatment may last months or become chronic.

confused_with: Normal grief or bereavement — both involve sadness, but grief typically comes in waves tied to reminders of loss, while depression is more persistent and pervasive with marked guilt, worthlessness, and functional impairment beyond what's expected in mourning.
Adjustment disorder — triggered by an identifiable stressor and improves as the person adapts, whereas depression meets full symptom criteria and often persists regardless of life circumstances.

Bipolar depression — looks identical during a depressive episode, but a history of even brief periods of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep with high energy, or unusual goal-directed activity points to bipolar disorder; this distinction changes treatment since antidepressants alone can worsen bipolar course.
Hypothyroidism or other medical conditions — can cause fatigue, weight gain, and low mood but lack the pervasive anhedonia and guilt; thyroid testing and medical workup clarify.

Burnout or chronic stress — involves exhaustion and cynicism specific to work or caregiving roles, but doesn't usually include the early-morning awakening, worthlessness, suicidal thoughts, or global loss of pleasure seen in depression.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: A detailed timeline of symptom onset, duration, and triggers; screening for past mood elevation; medical and substance history; assessment of guilt, anhedonia, and suicidality which are more specific to depression.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: Grief and adjustment disorder generally improve over weeks to months and fluctuate with reminders or stressor resolution. Depression persists for weeks to months without clear improvement and can recur even after full recovery.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Grief allows for moments of positive emotion and connection; adjustment disorder causes distress but often preserves function in unrelated domains. Depression typically causes global withdrawal, pervasive inability to experience pleasure, and significant impairment across all life areas.

description.overview: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes involving persistent low mood and/or anhedonia with associated cognitive, neurovegetative, and psychomotor changes causing clinically significant distress or impairment. Episodes are not attributable to a substance or another medical condition and are not better explained by other primary psychiatric disorders.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A graphic designer who always met deadlines starts missing client meetings and leaving projects half-finished. She stops returning emails, cancels lunch plans with friends, and spends evenings lying on the couch unable to choose what to watch. Her apartment fills with takeout containers because cooking feels overwhelming.

A ninth-grader who loved drama club suddenly refuses to audition for the spring play and starts skipping rehearsals. His parents notice he's irritable at breakfast, sleeping past noon on weekends, and his grades slip from B's to failing. He tells his mom to stop asking if he's okay because nothing's wrong, he just doesn't care anymore.

A usually upbeat 45-year-old nurse begins calling out sick frequently, citing headaches and exhaustion. Coworkers notice she's quiet during breaks and no longer shares stories about her kids. At home, she snaps at her spouse over minor things, stops cooking family dinners, and spends hours scrolling her phone in bed. She tells herself she's just tired, but the fatigue never lifts.

A retired veteran who loved woodworking leaves his tools untouched for weeks and stops attending his weekly poker game. His daughter visits and finds him unshaven, the house cluttered, and the fridge nearly empty. When she asks what's going on, he says he doesn't see the point in anything anymore and wishes he could just sleep and not wake up.

A 23-year-old graduate student who was passionate about research stops going to the lab and doesn't respond to her advisor's emails. She sleeps 14 hours a day but still feels exhausted. Her roommate notices she's lost weight and rarely leaves her room. When friends invite her out, she declines, thinking they'd be better off without her.

A small business owner who built his company from the ground up starts arriving late, leaving early, and delegating everything. He stops exercising, gains weight, and drinks more in the evenings. His partner notices he's withdrawn and irritable, and when asked, he says he feels like a failure despite objective success. He begins to think his family would be better off if he weren't around.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that their struggles have a name and aren't just personal weakness or laziness.
Fear or shame about being labeled with a mental health condition and what others might think.
Skepticism that this is 'real' or that treatment will actually help.
Frustration that there's no quick fix and that recovery may take time.
Hope that understanding what's happening means they can finally start to feel better.
Guilt about how their symptoms have affected loved ones and responsibilities.

first_person_statements: I woke up every day feeling like I was carrying a hundred-pound weight on my chest, and even brushing my teeth felt like an impossible task.
I couldn't remember the last time I laughed or looked forward to anything. Everything just felt gray and pointless.
I convinced myself everyone would be better off without me, that I was just a burden dragging everyone down.
I'd lie awake until 4 a.m. with my mind racing about everything I'd screwed up, then sleep through my alarms and miss work.
People kept telling me to just cheer up or think positive, but they didn't understand that my brain wouldn't let me feel anything good anymore.
I isolated myself because I didn't want to bring others down, but the loneliness made everything so much worse.

comparisons: Imagine waking up every day with the emotional equivalent of a severe flu: everything takes enormous effort, you can't enjoy your favorite foods or activities, and you feel isolated even in a room full of people.
It's like living in a house where all the lights have dimmed and the color has drained from everything you used to love, and no amount of willpower can flip the switch back on.
Think of it as your brain's threat detection system stuck in overdrive, constantly telling you that you're failing, you're worthless, and nothing will get better, even when there's no real danger.
It's like running on a treadmill that keeps speeding up: you're exhausted, falling behind, and can't see a way to stop or step off, while everyone around you seems to be walking effortlessly.

faqs.question: Major depression vs. persistent depressive disorder: what's the difference?
faqs.answer: Major depression involves distinct episodes of at least two weeks with intense symptoms and marked impairment. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves a chronic low-grade depressed mood lasting at least two years with fewer symptoms, though major depressive episodes can occur on top of it.

faqs.question: Can you have major depression and anxiety at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, anxiety disorders and major depression co-occur very frequently. Many people experience both persistent worry or panic alongside depressed mood and anhedonia, and addressing both conditions together often improves outcomes.

faqs.question: Major depression vs. bipolar depression: how are they different?
faqs.answer: During a depressive episode, they can look identical. The key difference is that bipolar disorder also involves episodes of mania or hypomania (elevated mood, decreased sleep need, increased energy or risk-taking). This distinction is critical because treatment differs: antidepressants alone in bipolar disorder can trigger mood instability.

faqs.question: Major depression vs. grief: how do you tell them apart?
faqs.answer: Grief typically comes in waves tied to reminders of the loss and allows for moments of positive emotion and connection. Major depression is more constant and pervasive, with profound guilt, worthlessness, and inability to experience pleasure that goes beyond what's expected in normal bereavement.

faqs.question: Sadness vs. major depression: what's the difference?
faqs.answer: Sadness is a normal emotion that everyone experiences in response to disappointments or losses. Major depression involves persistent low mood or anhedonia lasting at least two weeks, along with multiple other symptoms like sleep changes, guilt, fatigue, and impaired functioning, and it doesn't resolve with usual coping or time.

faqs.question: Adjustment disorder vs. major depression: how do you tell them apart?
faqs.answer: Adjustment disorder develops in response to a specific identifiable stressor and typically improves as the person adapts or the stressor resolves. Major depression meets full diagnostic criteria with multiple symptoms, can occur without a clear trigger, and persists regardless of life circumstances. Depression also causes more pervasive impairment across all life domains.

faqs.question: Can major depression be caused by a chemical imbalance?
faqs.answer: Depression involves complex changes in brain chemistry, circuitry, and stress systems, not a simple 'chemical imbalance.' Genetics, life stress, trauma, medical illness, and sleep all interact to alter brain function. The chemical imbalance model is an oversimplification, though medications that affect neurotransmitters can help many people.

faqs.question: Does major depression ever go away on its own?
faqs.answer: Some episodes may improve over months without treatment, but untreated depression often lasts longer, causes more impairment, and increases risk of recurrence and suicide. Early, effective treatment leads to faster recovery and better long-term outcomes.

faqs.question: Can you fully recover from major depression?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people achieve full remission and return to their previous level of functioning with treatment. However, depression can be recurrent, so ongoing attention to sleep, stress, and early warning signs, and sometimes maintenance treatment, helps prevent relapse.

faqs.question: How long does a major depressive episode last?
faqs.answer: Without treatment, episodes can last several months or longer. With effective treatment, many people see significant improvement within weeks to a couple of months, though full remission may take longer.

faqs.question: What triggers a major depressive episode?
faqs.answer: Episodes can be triggered by major life stressors (loss, trauma, relationship or job changes), chronic stress, medical illness, substance use, or sleep disruption. In some people, especially after recurrent episodes, depression can occur without an obvious trigger.

faqs.question: Is major depression genetic?
faqs.answer: There is a genetic component: having a first-degree relative with depression increases risk. However, it's not a single gene but many genetic variants interacting with life experiences, stress, and environmental factors.

faqs.question: Can major depression cause physical symptoms?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Depression commonly causes fatigue, sleep disturbances, appetite and weight changes, body aches, headaches, and digestive issues. Some people present to their doctor primarily with physical complaints before mood symptoms are recognized.

faqs.question: Can you work or go to school with major depression?
faqs.answer: It depends on severity. Mild to moderate depression may allow continued work or school with accommodations and treatment, though performance often suffers. Severe depression can make it very difficult or impossible to function in these roles until symptoms improve.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a major depressive episode and a major depressive disorder?
faqs.answer: A major depressive episode is a period of at least two weeks with specific symptoms. Major depressive disorder is the diagnosis given when someone has had one or more such episodes and the criteria for other conditions (like bipolar disorder) aren't met.

faqs.question: Can therapy alone treat major depression?
faqs.answer: For mild to moderate depression, evidence-based psychotherapy like CBT or IPT can be very effective as a standalone treatment. For moderate to severe depression, combining therapy with medication often works better than either alone.

faqs.question: How do antidepressants work for major depression?
faqs.answer: Antidepressants affect brain neurotransmitters like serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which over weeks can help restore normal mood regulation, improve sleep and energy, and reduce negative thinking. They're part of a broader treatment plan that includes therapy and lifestyle changes.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think I have major depression?
faqs.answer: Talk to your primary care doctor or a mental health professional. They can assess your symptoms, rule out medical causes, and discuss treatment options. If you're having thoughts of self-harm or suicide, seek help immediately through a crisis line, emergency room, or 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

faqs.question: Can major depression come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, recurrence is common, especially if someone has had multiple episodes. Maintenance treatment (ongoing therapy and/or medication), attention to sleep and stress, and recognizing early warning signs can reduce the risk of relapse.

faqs.question: Is major depression a disability?
faqs.answer: Major depression can be disabling, especially when severe or recurrent. It may qualify for workplace accommodations under the ADA or disability benefits if it substantially limits major life activities, though this depends on individual circumstances and documentation.
